transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2027-04-25 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~46 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Redwood CSM); Nina Patel, Omar Reid, Sofia Kim (Verdant Systems)

Summary:
Quick weekly pilot sync to review yesterday's throughput run, diagnose recurring queue spikes during 2x burst windows, agree on concurrency and batch targets, and align next steps for canary ramp and security artifacts. Customer emphasized desire for steady p99 under 200ms while keeping cost within projected budget.

Topics covered:
- Yesterday's throughput results and anomalies
- Continuous batching behavior and KV cache hit rates
- Queue backpressure and queue_depth tuning (latency buckets)
- Concurrency targets vs tail-latency tradeoffs
- Canary plan and cost estimates
- Security and audit artifacts for pilot progression

High level action items (short):
- Run longer throughput test at new params
- Customer to produce spike profile
- Redwood to share docs and runbook snippets

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call, good to see you. Nina, Omar, Sofia, you there?
[00:06] Nina Patel: Yup, hi. Sorry running a bit behind morning for us.
[00:08] Omar Reid: Here. All good.
[00:10] Diego Alvarez: Hey team, Diego from Redwood, I'll lead the tuning notes today.
[00:13] Maya Chen: Cool. Quick agenda — results review, identify spikes, adjust concurrency/batch, next steps. Does that work?
[00:18] Sofia Kim: Sounds good. We're excited to get the canary scheduled.

[03:10] Diego Alvarez: Ok so walking through the run from yesterday — we did a 6 hour run with synthetic traffic modeled off your prod percentiles. Average TPS was about 820 tokens/sec across the pool, with steady KV cache hit around 72%. Batch target set to 12, concurrency target 60.
[03:32] Nina Patel: Right and overall throughput matched expectations but we saw those intermittent p99 blips — around 250 to 340ms for short windows, mostly during your double-burst at minute markers ~14, 27, 41.
[03:47] Diego Alvarez: Exactly. Looking at traces the backpressure event correlates with queue depth growth — requests piling for ~120-200ms before being batched and scheduled. There's also a small GC-like pause on one of the worker nodes, though the runtime's metrics are fuzzy — sometimes the telemetry tag names swapped (we saw kvcache miss labelled as kv_cach in the agent output).
[04:10] Omar Reid: Hm ok so what's our quick knob to reduce those p99 spikes without burning cost? If we crank concurrency we'll increase tail a bit but reduce queueing?
[04:20] Diego Alvarez: Right tradeoff. Two levers: increase concurrency (more in-flight model contexts) and raise continuous batching aggressiveness (so batches fill faster). But raising concurrency can increase memory and KV cache pressure — which lowers hit rate and increases per-token cost.
[04:39] Maya Chen: Also we can tweak the queue admission — have short circuit for small requests (like < 64 tokens) to bypass heavy batching to keep latency tight.

[06:05] Nina Patel: Could you remind me of the exact config names again? We used concurrency_target, continuous_batch_window_ms, batch_target?
[06:12] Diego Alvarez: Yes: concurrency_target=60, continuous_batch_window_ms=30ms (we had set 20ms initially then bumped to 30 during the run), batch_target=12. There's also queue_depth_limit and queue_preempt_ms for urgent path.
[06:30] Nina Patel: Ok that helps.

[09:50] Diego Alvarez: Looking at the heatmaps: when traffic hits 2x bursts, effective batching latency increases because more requests are queueing then a single worker becomes the bottleneck. Two mitigations: distribute requests across more serving shards (adds infra cost) or introduce burst capacity fallback to a larger but slightly cheaper model variant that has lower latency per token.
[10:10] Sofia Kim: We were hoping to avoid spinning more instances during pilot — budget constraint. How big is the cost delta for fallback variant?
[10:18] Maya Chen: We estimated fallback adds roughly 18-25% to throughput cost but can reduce tail by 40-60% during spikes depending on model. We'll send a more precise cost sheet.

[11:40] Omar Reid: On KV cache — you said hit rate was 72%. Any quick changes to push that to 85%?
[11:47] Diego Alvarez: Cache pressure is mostly from concurrency and cold-keys during spikes. Increasing per-shard cache size helps but again memory. We also have prefix-caching heuristics — e.g., pin initial conversation tokens in hot cache for the session length you described — that can improve effective hit rate without changing memory too much.
[12:10] Nina Patel: That could be useful, our chat flows tend to have long shared prefixes.

[14:55] Diego Alvarez: For the next run proposal: concurrency_target=80, batch_target=16, continuous_batch_window_ms=25ms, queue_depth_limit=150 (ms) and turn on prefix pinning for sessions. That should smooth the queue growth and keep p99 closer to 180-200ms.
[15:14] Nina Patel: 80 seems high relative to our mem constraints — we'll need to validate on our side that the customer nodes can handle 80 in-flight contexts per GPU.
[15:22] Omar Reid: Can Redwood simulate memory pressure so we can see when KV eviction will happen?
[15:28] Diego Alvarez: We can instrument a synthetic run that forces eviction patterns; I'll include eviction histograms in the CSV.

[18:00] Maya Chen: Quick question on observability — Priya, did you find the per-request token-level breakdown in the console when Diego uploaded the run?
[18:08] Priya Rao: Yes it's visible but some labels were off — streaming chunk size was reported as 128 when in config it's 64; we flagged it as mapping mismatch. Should be a quick fix.

[21:10] Nina Patel: About canary plan, we want to start with 5% traffic for two days, then 10% for two days, provided p99 stays under 200ms. Anything else we should lock?
[21:22] Maya Chen: That plan looks good. We'll also bake in automatic fallback if p99 goes above 250ms for three consecutive 15min windows — we can trigger fallback to fallback-variant or bump capacity.
[21:34] Diego Alvarez: We'll create an automated SLO alert that fires on p99>250ms and an Action: auto-scale or switch variant.

[23:05] Omar Reid: Security check: we need the SOC2 artifact and a network diagram for the private peering setup. Timelines?
[23:12] Maya Chen: I'll share the SOC2 summary and network whitepaper by Monday. For private peering diagrams we have templates; we can adapt to Verdant's VPC setup.
[23:25] Sofia Kim: Can you include KMS/HSM specifics? Our compliance team asks about key rotation and HSM-backed signing.
[23:33] Maya Chen: Yes — we'll include KMS integration notes and key rotation cadence.

[26:45] Diego Alvarez: Back to tuning — a smaller change we recommend now: enable queue_preempt_ms=40ms so high-priority short requests are pulled forward. That reduces p50 significantly and helps p95 during bursts.
[26:58] Nina Patel: Will that starve longer generation jobs? We do have 60% of traffic that's short queries but the rest are long.
[27:06] Diego Alvarez: We can set a dual-queue mechanism — low-latency path for short tokens and best-effort for longer requests. Thresholds configurable based on token count.

[30:40] Nina Patel: For the longer run you suggested, what's the telemetry you'll produce? I want p50/p95/p99, queue_wait_time histogram, kvcache hit/miss over time, per-shard eviction rates, and cost estimate per million tokens.
[30:51] Diego Alvarez: Yes we'll produce all that and attach raw CSVs. We'll also include a sample flamegraph of the runtime during a spike window.

[33:20] Sofia Kim: One more ask — can we get a simple guidance table: if we raise concurrency by X then expect Y change in p99 and Z change in cost? Even approximate is fine.
[33:30] Maya Chen: We'll prepare a guidance table — Diego will run a few param sweeps and produce approximate deltas.

[35:00] Diego Alvarez: Quick note about model variants: some variants are quantized and cheaper but have longer per-token decode time in some lengths; others have faster kernel paths for short sequences. We'll match variant to your request length mix.
[35:15] Omar Reid: Ok.

[36:20] Nina Patel: Anything else on the instrumentation side we should enable now?
[36:24] Priya Rao: We suggest turning on request-level tracing for the canary (1:10 sampling), and include a trace-id forwarded to your APM so you can join traces with backend.
[36:33] Diego Alvarez: That also helps diagnose cross-service stalls that look like runtime GC but are actually network or APM sampling artefact.

[39:10] Maya Chen: Let's recap decisions — run a 24h stress at concurrency 80, batch target 16, continuous batch window 25ms, enable prefix pinning and queue_preempt 40ms; Verdant will provide spike profile; Redwood will send SOC2/whitepaper and cost estimates; schedule canary on Wednesday next week at 10:00 UTC.
[39:30] Sofia Kim: That all checks out from our side pending the memory validation and the spike profile.
[39:36] Omar Reid: We'll validate memory and respond by Thursday.

[41:10] Diego Alvarez: I'll kick off the 24h run this afternoon and share CSVs; expect initial artifacts in about 18 hours.
[41:20] Maya Chen: I'll attach the security docs and the cost sheet.

[43:00] Nina Patel: Thanks everyone — very helpful.
[43:04] Maya Chen: Thanks — we'll follow up with the run outputs and update calendar for the canary.
[43:10] Priya Rao: Ping us if anything urgent.
[43:14] Sofia Kim: Bye all.

End of transcript
